The Potato Eaters. Vincent van Gogh's 1885 painting depicts a family of peasants gathered around a table in dim lamplight, eating a meagre meal of potatoes. This is van Gogh's early masterpiece—a study in earthy colour, social empathy, and the dignity of labour rendered through expressive brushwork and psychological intensity.

Van Gogh spent weeks sketching and studying the Potato Eaters family in their cottage in Nuenen in northern Brabant, returning repeatedly to capture the right moment and emotional truth. The painting's palette is deliberately dark and muted—browns, ochres, and sombre greens—to convey both the poverty of the scene and the spiritual gravitas van Gogh perceived in peasant life. Five figures lean inward around a table illuminated by a single hanging lamp; the light models their weathered faces with an almost Rembrandtian chiaroscuro.

The painting measures approximately 82 by 114 centimetres, and multiple versions and studies exist, including a lithograph. Van Gogh called it "the best thing I have ever done" at the time, though it sold only after his death, when critics recognised its emotional and formal power. The work now hangs in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam and marks his evolution from dark Realism toward the colour-saturated Post-Impressionism he would later embrace, demonstrating the movement's emotional intensity and his deep sympathy for rural labour and the marginalised.
